chapters.title: Chapter 6: Backtesting and the Traps That Break Trend and Momentum Strategies

lessons.title: Survivorship Bias, Look-Ahead Bias, and Data Snooping

children.text: This course has flagged backtesting problems in nearly every chapter without naming them precisely: Chapter 2's curve-fitting warning, Chapter 4's point about the Jegadeesh-Titman grid being credible because it held up across every combination, Chapter 5's caution about hypothetical case studies. This lesson names the three most common, most damaging traps directly: survivorship bias, look-ahead bias, and data snooping. Each one makes a backtest look better than a real, live deployment ever would, through a completely different mechanism.

body.text: A backtest can be technically bug-free and still be worthless, if it tests on a stock universe that quietly excludes the failures, uses information that wasn't actually available at the time, or is one lucky result out of many unreported attempts. None of these show up as an error message. All three inflate a strategy's apparent quality.

children.text: Survivorship Bias: Testing Only on Winners

markDefs.definition: The distortion that results from testing a strategy only on entities that still exist today, silently excluding companies that failed, delisted, or were removed from an index, which flatters historical results.

children.text: creeps in the moment a backtest uses today's list of Nifty 200 constituents to test a strategy across the last ten or fifteen years. Any company that was in that universe at some point but was later delisted, went bankrupt, or was removed from the index for poor performance, is invisible to that test. Satyam Computer Services, a Nifty 50 constituent until its accounting fraud came to light in January 2009, is a well-known real example: a backtest built from today's index membership would never have included Satyam at all, quietly erasing one of the more dramatic single-stock collapses in Indian market history from the test data. A momentum strategy backtested this way looks better than it would have performed in reality, since it never had the chance to be caught holding a stock that later fell to zero.
Look-Ahead Bias: Using Information You Didn't Actually Have Yet

markDefs.definition: The distortion that results from a backtest using data or information that would not actually have been available at the historical moment a trading decision was simulated.

children.text: is subtler and specifically dangerous for momentum backtesting. The most common version: using a stock's current index membership to decide which stocks were 'in the universe' at every past rebalance date, rather than that index's actual, point-in-time historical membership. A stock added to the Nifty 200 in 2023 should not appear in a backtest's rankings for 2019, even though it is a Nifty 200 constituent today. A second, equally common version involves financial data itself: quarterly results are often revised in the weeks after their first release, and using the final, restated figures as if they were available on the original result date silently gives a backtest information it would never have had in real time.

body.text: Point-in-time data, historical index membership as it actually stood on each date, and financial data as first reported rather than later restated, is genuinely harder to source than a simple current snapshot. That difficulty is exactly why look-ahead bias is so common: the easy version of the data is also the biased version.

children.text: Data Snooping: When Enough Trials Guarantee a 'Discovery'

markDefs.definition: The distortion that results from testing many strategies or parameter combinations on the same historical data and reporting only the best-performing one, without disclosing the full set of attempts.

children.text: , also called multiple testing, is the statistical version of the curve-fitting warning from Chapter 2. Every parameter a strategy has, an SMA window, a slope lookback, a band size, is effectively another chance to stumble onto a combination that happens to look good on the specific historical sample tested, purely by chance, with no real edge behind it. The more combinations tested, the more likely at least one will look impressive for reasons that have nothing to do with a genuine, repeatable edge.

body.caption: If n independent, genuinely worthless strategies are each tested at a significance threshold alpha, this is the probability that at least one of them appears statistically significant purely by chance.
Probability of at least one false positive at a 5% significance threshold (alpha = 0.05)

body.text: Test 100 completely random, genuinely worthless trading rules on the same historical data, and by simple probability, roughly 99.4% of the time at least one of them will appear statistically significant at the conventional 5% threshold. If a researcher, or a course, tests 100 parameter combinations and reports only the single best-looking one without disclosing the other 99, that result tells you almost nothing about whether a real edge exists.

body.caption: Simulating data snooping: finding a 'winner' among pure noise
body.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=42)

# 100 completely random "strategies": each is just noise, no real edge
n_strategies = 100
n_days = 500
sharpe_ratios = []

for _ in range(n_strategies):
    daily_returns = rng.normal(loc=0.0, scale=0.01, size=n_days)  # zero true edge
    sharpe = daily_returns.mean() / daily_returns.std() * np.sqrt(252)
    sharpe_ratios.append(sharpe)

sharpe_ratios = np.array(sharpe_ratios)
print(f"Best Sharpe ratio out of {n_strategies} random, edge-free strategies: {sharpe_ratios.max():.2f}")
print(f"Average Sharpe ratio across all {n_strategies}: {sharpe_ratios.mean():.2f}")

body.text: Run this simulation and the 'best' Sharpe ratio out of 100 pure-noise strategies typically lands well above 1.0, a figure that would look genuinely impressive presented on its own, even though every single strategy in the simulation was built from random numbers with zero real edge by construction. This is data snooping made visible: the best of many worthless attempts can look indistinguishable from a real discovery.

body.title: Spot the bias
body.question: A researcher backtests a momentum strategy on 'all current Nifty 200 stocks' going back to 2015, using each stock's full price history over that period. What bias does this most directly introduce?
options: Look-ahead bias, because future prices are used to make past decisions
Survivorship bias, because stocks that were removed from the index or delisted between 2015 and today are excluded from the test entirely
Data snooping, because only one strategy was tested
No bias, since real historical prices were used throughout
body.explanation: Using today's Nifty 200 membership list to define the backtest universe across past years silently excludes every stock that was removed or delisted along the way, the defining mechanism of survivorship bias, even though the price data itself is genuinely historical.

body.title: Calculate the false-positive probability
body.prompt: If 30 independent, genuinely worthless strategies are each tested at a 5% significance threshold, what is the probability that at least one appears statistically significant purely by chance? Give your answer as a percentage, to 1 decimal place.
body.explanation: 1 - (1 - 0.05)^30 = 1 - 0.95^30 = 1 - 0.2146 = 0.7854, or 78.5%. Even without deliberately cherry-picking, testing 30 parameter combinations makes a spurious-looking 'significant' result more likely than not.

body.title: Reviewing a backtest claim
body.scenario: A vendor pitches a momentum trading system, claiming a backtested Sharpe ratio of 2.1 over the last 10 years on the Nifty 500. When you ask what universe was used, they say 'the current Nifty 500 list,' and when you ask how many parameter combinations were tested before arriving at the final version, they decline to answer.
body.prompt: Based on this lesson, what two specific concerns would you raise before trusting this Sharpe ratio?
body.modelAnswer: First, using the current Nifty 500 list for a 10-year backtest almost certainly introduces survivorship bias, since any stock that was removed from the index or delisted over that decade is silently excluded, inflating the apparent result. Second, the vendor's refusal to disclose how many parameter combinations were tested before settling on this one is a data snooping red flag, if dozens or hundreds of variations were tried, a Sharpe ratio of 2.1 could easily be the best of many worthless attempts rather than evidence of a genuine, repeatable edge. Both issues would need to be resolved, point-in-time universe data and full disclosure of the search process, before the headline number means anything.

body.label: Search for point-in-time index membership data via NSE's official archives
body.description: Properly avoiding survivorship and look-ahead bias requires point-in-time index membership history, which NSE's own archives and historical circulars are a starting point for sourcing, rather than relying on a current constituent list alone.

cards.definition: The distortion from testing only on entities that still exist today, silently excluding companies that failed, delisted, or were removed from an index.
The distortion from a backtest using data or information that would not actually have been available at the historical moment a decision was simulated.
The distortion from testing many strategies or parameter combinations on the same data and reporting only the best-performing one.
Historical data, such as index membership or financial results, recorded as it genuinely stood on each historical date, rather than as it appears today.

points: Survivorship bias comes from testing on today's stock universe applied to past dates, silently excluding delisted or removed companies like Satyam Computer Services, and flatters historical results.
Look-ahead bias comes from using information that would not actually have been available at the time, including current index membership applied to past dates and restated financial data.

Data snooping comes from testing many strategies or parameter combinations and reporting only the best one, which can produce an impressive-looking result from pure statistical chance alone, as the simulation in this lesson demonstrated directly.
The probability of at least one false positive rises sharply with the number of combinations tested, from 5% with a single test to over 99% with 100 tests, at a standard 5% significance threshold.
None of these biases show up as a bug or an error. A technically correct backtest can still be seriously misleading if it falls into any of these three traps.
